Use the routing engine as a structured baseline, then predict its residual from current traffic, road segments, pickup/dropoff conditions, and recent execution errors. This makes the learned target smaller and preserves physical route information, though directly predicting total time can be appropriate when the baseline is poor. Do not state residual learning as a universal requirement.

For delivery, separately model travel, restaurant preparation, courier wait, and handoff; their dependencies matter when combining forecasts. Availability of restaurant/courier signals must match the prediction timestamp. Streaming updates should refresh predictions as events arrive without leaking the actual final completion time into training.

If lateness is more costly than earliness, predict an appropriate conditional quantile with pinball loss instead of only the mean. Report quantile coverage and sharpness by geography, merchant, time of day, and trip length. Use fallback routing estimates for missing ML features and monitor systematic residual drift after road/network changes. Validate promised-time impact on cancellations and satisfaction, not only average absolute error.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Quantile regression minimizes pinball loss $\rho_\tau(u)=u(\tau-\mathbf1[u<0])$ for residual $u=y-\hat y$. Choosing a higher quantile accounts for asymmetric lateness costs, but promised-time policies should be evaluated end to end. Check empirical interval/quantile coverage by geography and time, not only pooled MAE. [3](https://otexts.com/fpp3/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://www.uber.com/blog/deepeta-how-uber-predicts-arrival-times/) and [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_quantile_regression.html).
